content.thinking:
I need to write the postmortem using placeholder names for all figures rather than inventing numbers myself—duration, error rates before/while/peak should all reference named variables. I'm building out the causal chain starting with the symptom of failed account page requests citing the relevant sources, then tracing why into the PaymentProviderFailed error.

The trace continues down to the io-pay 503 and the synchronous call in payment_provider.py:95 with no fallback handling, then stops there since the record can't explain why io-pay itself returned 503—I should stick to only what evidence supports rather than speculating further. I'm noting the actions taken (Argus refusing to act, moving to fixing, drafting a PR, escalating) while being careful to flag that the PR's actual content is unknown and shouldn't be assumed to fully address the issue. For contributing factors, I'm flagging the lack of graceful degradation as needing a new action item, along with Argus's lack of mitigation for upstream failures, and considering whether the gap between alert time and incident onset constitutes a detection lag worth calling out as its own contributing factor.

Now I'm landing on three concrete action items: AI-2 for mitigation (render the account page without card details when io-pay fails, using a timeout or circuit breaker), AI-3 for detection (alert directly on io-pay's 503 rate or add a synthetic probe), and AI-4 for process (a runbook for third-party outages plus an established contact point with io-pay's status page). I'm also deciding to avoid stating exact numbers in the summary, using phrasing like "at least" for duration instead, and considering whether to note any lucky aspects of the incident, though I'm uncertain if that's worth including given the limited evidence.

For what went well, Argus deserves credit for catching the alert and forming an investigation candidate quickly. For what went wrong, the service never actually recovered, Argus never attempted mitigation, and there was a real detection lag between when the issue began and when the alert fired.

action_items.item: Make the account page tolerate an io-pay failure. Put a short timeout and a circuit breaker on the provider client, and render the page without card details when the lookup fails.

Alert on the rate of 503 responses from io-pay in the payment provider client, and add a synthetic probe of the provider, so a provider outage is flagged separately and sooner than the aggregate io-shop error rate.

Write a runbook and a prepared control, such as a flag that hides the card section, for third-party provider outages. Include contacting io-pay and checking its status page, so Argus or the on-call engineer has a mitigation to apply.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw account page requests fail. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, starting at {began}. The service was still failing at the last minute of metrics read.

The account page requests were failing with PaymentProviderFailed, raised in the payment provider client when io-pay returned 503 for the shopper card lookup. These errors began in the same minute as the onset and peaked during the outage.
A failed io-pay call failed the whole account page request. The page depends on the card lookup while it renders, and the error is raised from the provider client with no fallback or degraded page.

io-pay itself began returning 503 at {began}. Nothing on io-shop's side changed beforehand: there were no production changes and no flag changes. The replicas were all running as before, so the fault lay in the third-party dependency.
The record does not say why io-pay failed, because it is an external provider and no evidence from its side was available. The chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The account page has no degraded mode. When the card lookup fails, the whole page fails instead of rendering without the card details.
Argus has no mitigation for a third-party dependency failure. It refused to act and could only propose a code change, so the outage continued while the incident was escalated.
Detection relied on the aggregate error-rate alert, which was raised at {alert_raised}, well after the onset at {began}. Nothing watched io-pay's 503 rate directly.

input.executive_summary: From {began}, most requests for shoppers' account pages on io-shop failed. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The service had not recovered by the last minute of metrics read, so the outage lasted at least {duration}, and that is a lower bound. The cause was the external payment provider io-pay returning errors. The account page needs io-pay to render and had no fallback. No deploy, release or flag change preceded the onset. Argus has no safe automated action for a third-party outage, so it opened a draft pull request and escalated to a human, who must review it (AI-1). Argus held the incident for {held}. That measures the response, not the outage.

went_well: Argus picked up the alert within seconds, read metrics, logs, changes and flag history, and identified an upstream dependency failure as the leading candidate with no internal change to blame.
Argus did not take a mitigation that would not have helped, and it escalated with a draft pull request open.
went_wrong: The service was still broken when the incident was escalated. Nothing Argus could do answered this kind of failure.
The leading candidate was never tried or confirmed, and the record has no evidence from io-pay's side.
The account page fails completely when one dependency fails.

input.root_cause: The io-shop account page calls the third-party payment provider (io-pay) synchronously, and from {began} io-pay returned 503 for the shopper card lookup. io-shop had no fallback for that failure, so the provider's errors became account page errors. The record does not show why io-pay failed.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for most shoppers
